text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden's opposition conservative party, The Moderates, is the most widely popular party in Sweden now winning 31.5 percent of support in the latest poll by Dagens Nyheter and Temo. The February poll found the ruling Social Democrats lost some support after an energy agreement with the Centre and Left parties to phase out nuclear power. Its popularity slipped to the lowest level in six years -- 27 percent.
- More cooperation between airline SAS and other alliances is not only logical but necessary under European Union rules. More competition on regional airlines is necessary,

- Steel company SSAB surprised the market, posting a profit of 2.1 billion crowns due to a strong development during the fourth quarter of 1996 which was several hundred million crown higher than the market expected.

- A nine-member airline alliance to compete with British Airways and American Airlines would reduce competition and could result in higher ticket prices. The plans are not entirely clear but negotiations are continuing, reports say.
- The North American market is becoming more important for Atlas Copco, which posted a eight percent higher profit in 1996 over a year earlier.
- Finnish telecoms group Nokia Oy's results were in line with market expectations.

- Sweden's Skandia is preparing to sell off its rapidly expanding international assurance business, a global operation which made a profit last year of over 1.1 billion crowns. Assurance and Financial Services managing director Jan Carendi said the process of preparation for the stock market is already underway but nothing firm decided.

- Industry and Commerce Minister Leif Pagrotsky has reacted furiously to suggestions by Handelsbanken chairman Tom Hedelius that some of the country's top companies should consider moving their head offices abroad. Pagrotsky, who became industry and commerce minister two weeks ago, said this showed a lack of respect for democracy.

- Swedes are sinking money into various types of savings funds at record levels. In January alone more the 14 billion crowns were invested in funds which almost equals total new savings during all of 1996.

- The Swedish government on Thursday set up a commission to try to trace the gold bought by Sweden's government and banks from Nazi Germany during World War Two. The commission will review bank accounts established by persecuted European Jews prior to the start of the war.
